newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus sign scaled-down Union Treaty.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus sign scaled-down Union Treaty.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin signed a scaled-down Union Treaty on Wednesday with Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko after intervention by liberals in Moscow opposed to full integration with Russia's controversial western neighbour.

"The union does not create a single state. Each side maintains its sovereignty. At the same time it takes our integration onto a qualitatively new phase," Yeltsin said in the Kremlin before the signing ceremony.

The accord is designed to build on a "community treaty" signed exactly a year ago when Yeltsin, then running for re-election, sought to appeal to the widespread nostalgia among Russian voters for the Soviet Union which collapsed in 1991.
But it was far shorter than the document backed by Lukashenko, who wants to unite his struggling 10 million strong former Soviet republic with the vast Russian Federation.

The 17-page draft was reduced to three at 11th hour talks, and many details appeared to have been transfered into a separate charter, initialled by the two presidents pending further reworking and public discussion during the next month.

Liberals in the Russian government had opposed the original draft, saying they feared union could harm Russia's economy and make Lukashenko, who once professed an admiration for Adolf Hitler, a key player in Moscow politics.
The new document "is much more thought-out than before, thanks to intelligent people," Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov told reporters at the Kremlin.

Reflecting the last minute bargaining, television pictures showed Belarussian and Russian officials working on some documents just minutes before the elaborate signing ceremony which was delayed by 30 minutes.

Yeltsin said the "Treaty on a Union of Belarus and Russia", gave citizens of the two countries freedom of movement and rights of residency, property ownership, and participation in local elections in both Belarus and Russia.

It also involved big savings on border guarding and defence and would make police work easier. But he said it would not interfere with the constitution of either state and did not for the moment involve monetary union.

"It is entirely in line with those norms which have existed for a long time in the countries of the European Union," Yeltsin said. "Democracy and respect for human rights is one of the bases of our union."

Lukashenko, popular among many of his countrymen, is locked in a bitter row with the West over his human rights record and distaste for market reforms. The Belarus police regularly arrest opposition demonstrators and have cracked down on the media.
Details of the treaty were not immediately available but Yeltsin made clear financial issues had been left out.
"We have a lot of work to do on creating a single currency as mentioned in the draft charter," he said, adding that debates on the charter would be outlined in media broadcasts.
"I hope that it will also help people to understand properly what kind of treaty we are signing today and what has been put into the charter -- more explicit, more detailed," Yeltsin said.

Existing integration efforts with Belarus, which include a separate customs agreement also involving Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, have become mired in problems, with Russian officials accusing Belarus of not playing by the rules.

Economists say that while Belarus offers Russia a strategic corridor to the West for lucrative energy supplies, its backward economy would weigh heavily on Russia, whose own economic transition is fraught with difficulties.

Lukashenko, who told a news conference on Friday he had signed the draft document and put it on Yeltsin's desk, put a brave face on the compromise on Wednesday, insisting that integration would go ahead and not be harmful.
"Sooner or later we will enter our common home where the people from two states -- Belarus and Russia -- will live together," he said.
